stories.primary_headline: They came to see Kolkata's famous pandals, but never returned home

primary_source.headline: They came to see Kolkata's famous pandals, but never returned home
primary_source.content: Kolkata: Pranjal Sarkar had no visible injuries anywhere else on his body. The only mark was that of a shoe on the left side of his face, a grim imprint of the brutal force of the footstep of an unknown person who may have unwittingly crushed the 13-year-old to death when the crowd surged at the Durga Puja pandal in Chorbagan in north-central Kolkata.Pranjal watched videos of the Chorbagan Sarbojanin Durgotsab Samiti’s pandal on social media. The 13-year-old might not have fully grasped the “Beyond Sound” theme conceived and brought to life by artist Susanta Shibani Paul, but the sight of Goddess Durga and her four children, Kartik, Ganesh, Lakshmi and Saraswati, seated on a crescent moon amid dim, celestial lighting, caught his imagination. He insisted that the pandal be a must-see when his parents, Anukul Sarkar and Priyanka Sarkar, brought him from Agarpara in the North 24 Parganas district to Kolkata on the second day of the autumn festival.Little did Pranjal or his parents know that a danger lurked beneath the pandal’s surreal ambience, one that would turn the family’s Durga Puja outing into an unimaginable tragedy.The boy was one of the 19 people killed in the stampede at the pandal on Saturday. His parents survived, though. “He would have left for a tour to Shillong today with my sister and brother-in-law. Instead, I had to see the lifeless body of my nephew,” Pranjal’s maternal uncle said in front of the mortuary of Kolkata Medical College and Hospital on Sunday. “My brother-in-law could save seven or eight other children, but not his own son.”Even as the autumn festival unfolded across West Bengal, the stampede cast a pall of gloom over the families of the deceased and their neighbourhoods, from Kolkata and the Hooghly, Purba Bardhaman, North 24 Parganas and Nadia districts of West Bengal to Muzaffarpur in Bihar, turning what should have been a time of celebration into one of mourning.Kolkata stampede: Families mourn loss of loved ones as evening of festivity turned into heartacheSriparna Poddar, a 27-year-old nurse at a hospital in Kolkata, was often the first person her neighbours in Baidyabati, Hooghly, approached for healthcare advice. But on Sunday, she lay dead among the other victims of the stampede, while her family and neighbours waited to take home her mortal remains.Sandeep Bej, another 13-year-old boy, wanted to stay in his village in Madhabdihi in Purba Bardhaman for the Durga Puja celebrations but, at the last moment, went to Kolkata with his mother, Tagar Bej, 37, to see some of the city's pandals. However, the mother-son duo died in the stampede. So did Tagar’s sister, Piyali. Sandeep’s sister, Agamani Bej, was injured. “They were expected to return to their village on Sunday. But now only their mortal remains will return.”Ram Biswas came from Chakdaha in Nadia with his wife, Arati Sarkar Biswas, for pandal-hopping in Kolkata. He survived the stampede at Chorbagan but could not save his wife. Recalling the horror, Ram said that the crowd surged into the pandal after the ropes restricting entry were removed when it started raining. “It was dark inside, and people rushing in knocked others to the ground. Arati and I fell. I somehow got up and tried to pull her to her feet, but I couldn’t. My wife died before my eyes. I could do nothing,” Ram said on Sunday.For Abhishek Srivastava and his 13-year-old son, Ayansh, the trip to Kolkata was meant to be their first experience of the city’s famed Durga Puja celebrations. The two travelled from Muzaffarpur in Bihar to visit relatives in Agarpara, West Bengal, and went pandal-hopping with family members on Saturday. But both died in the stampede.Tania Biswas and Barnali Haldar, both 17, had planned their Maha Saptami outing well in advance. The Class XI students from Gouranga Nagar in New Town were close friends who had decided to wear sarees for the occasion. They set out with five other friends to visit the city’s Durga Puja pandals, but the outing ended in tragedy in Chorbagan, where both died in the stampede.Barnali’s father, Binod Haldar, who ekes out a living by pulling a rickshaw around New Town, learnt of his daughter’s death while he was still working. Her friends called him, and he rushed to the hospital, only to find that his elder child had already died. He spent the night outside the hospital mortuary. “My world has ended,” he said in a trembling voice, with tears rolling down his cheeks. “There will never be a Durga Puja in our lives again.”
